extracted.intended_audience: citizens of New York and other voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution; readers interested in constitutional design and judicial procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative guidance on what provisions a national constitution should (and should not) include, focusing on jury trial rules, separation of jurisdictions, and whether a bill of rights is necessary. Addresses practical and theoretical limits of adopting state practices at the federal level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated powers exclude general authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of particular powers (as in the plan of the convention) excludes any pretension to a general legislative authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affirmative grant of special powers implies no general authority; when powers are enumerated the specification marks precise limits beyond which the legislature or judiciary cannot extend. Example: Congress's power extends only to enumerated cases; similarly federal judicial authority is confined to cases particularly specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal judicial jurisdiction limited to specified cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial authority of the federal judicatures, being declared to comprehend certain cases particularly specified, marks the precise limits beyond which the federal courts cannot extend their jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because objects of cognizance are enumerated, the specification would be nugatory if it did not exclude broader authority; this is a criterion for construing the scope of the national judiciary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury essential safeguard in criminal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial by jury in criminal cases is a valuable safeguard to liberty and is provided for in the proposed plan in an ample manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institution, aided by habeas corpus, protects against arbitrary impeachments, prosecutions, and punishments — the main engines of judicial despotism. The Constitution should secure jury trial for criminal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury in civil cases not abolished by the proposed Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan does not abolish civil jury trials; in controversies of general public interest the institution will remain as under State constitutions because many such causes remain exclusively under state tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many civil causes (land causes except interstate grant disputes, controversies between citizens of the same State, admiralty, equity matters) will remain with State courts and thus unaffected. The national judiciary's limited cognizance preserves state practice in most civil matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature retains power to prescribe mode of trial for civil causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A power to constitute courts is also a power to prescribe the mode of trial; even though criminal jury trial is required, the legislature still has discretion regarding juries in civil causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Constitution prescribes jury trial for criminal matters only, it does not abridge the legislature's power to adopt or decline jury methods for civil cases. Example hypothetical: if married women had no prior power to convey property, a specification of a particular mode would exclude other modes; but where power exists, specification does not exclude other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury trial unsuitable for causes requiring specialized legal expertise (e.g., prize causes, law of nations)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many cases in which a trial by jury is ineligible—particularly those concerning public peace with foreign nations, prize causes, or matters that require thorough knowledge of the laws and usages of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries may lack competence to handle nuanced questions of public policy or international law and may be swayed by impressions harmful to national interests, risking infringement of other nations' rights and provoking reprisals. Treaties and practice (e.g., appeals to high executive or council bodies) show prize cases are often decided outside ordinary jury procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of equity from law jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of equity jurisdiction from common-law jurisdiction is important; causes proper for courts of equity would be improperly committed to juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of equity deal with extraordinary cases that are exceptions to general rules and often require long, intricate investigation incompatible with jury trials. Uniting equity with law risks unsettling general rules, making each case special and undermining the jury institution by introducing complicated questions unsuitable for juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury trial as a check on corruption, though imperfect
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial by jury is an important security against corruption because a temporarily summoned jury is harder to corrupt than a standing magistracy, though there are vulnerabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sheriffs and clerks who summon or nominate jurors are standing officers who could be corrupted; sometimes it may be easier to corrupt some jurors than a bench. Yet requiring both court and jury increases obstacles to corruption: if jury verdicts seem wrong, courts may grant new trials, so corruption would often require suborning both institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutional wording referencing 'heretofore' state practice for federal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions like 'trial by jury shall be as heretofore' are senseless for the United States because there is no antecedent federal practice to which 'heretofore' could refer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal constitution cannot sensibly adopt an indeterminate phrase that relies on a pre-existing federal standard; such wording would be vague and inoperative because 'the United States, as such, is at this time altogether unknown' in terms of judiciary practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity required before adopting state standards for jury availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopting a rule that federal jury trials follow state practices (e.g., 'as in actions at common law') would produce capricious and disparate operation across the Union because states differ widely in the boundaries between common-law and equity jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because in some states common-law courts have equity jurisdiction or admiralty is tried with juries, the same cause might be tried with a jury in one state and not in another. Thus, a general constitutional regulation must await a uniform plan regarding jurisdictions, which is difficult to devise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury affects taxation only in mode of collection and officer conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial by jury cannot influence the amount, objects, or apportionment of taxes; its effect, if any, is limited to the mode of collection and the conduct of revenue officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue efficacy often depends on summary proceedings (distress and sale) rather than jury trials; jury-based recovery could be too slow and costly, undermining collection. Abuses by revenue officers are punishable as public offenses, and criminal jury trial affords protection against official extortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid establishing jury trial in 'all cases whatsoever' by constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing the trial by jury in all cases would be an error; no precedent supports universal constitutional establishment of jury trial for every case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of differing state institutions and the existence of cases unsuitable for juries (equity, admiralty, prize, specialized matters), a blanket constitutional rule would be impracticable and inadvisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated constitutional protections (examples supporting claim no bill of rights needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution already contains several important protections equivalent to bill-of-rights provisions, such as habeas corpus, prohibitions on bills of attainder and ex post facto laws, prohibition of titles of nobility, jury trial for criminal cases, and narrow rules for treason and impeachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Article I §9 clauses (habeas corpus, no bill of attainder, no ex post facto laws, no titles of nobility); Article III §2–3 (criminal jury trials, treason definition requiring two witnesses or confession, Congress to declare punishment but no corruption of blood beyond life); impeachment limits (removal and disqualification only, separate criminal processes remain). These provisions serve many functions attributed to a bill of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment penalties limited and criminal process preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment in cases of impeachment shall not extend further than removal and disqualification from office, and the impeached party remains liable to indictment, trial, judgment, and punishment according to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause preserves a separate criminal process and limits impeachment to political punishment; it is cited as part of constitutionally-protected procedure distinct from private criminal sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treason narrowly defined with stringent evidentiary requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Treason against the United States consists only in levying war or adhering to enemies and requires the testimony of two witnesses to the same overt act, or confession in open court for conviction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may declare punishment for treason but no attainder of treason shall work corruption of blood or forfeiture except during the life of the person attainted. This narrow definition protects against broad or oppressive readings of treason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial venue rule for crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial of all crimes, except impeachment, shall be by jury and held in the State where the crimes were committed; when not committed within any State, Congress shall direct the place of trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural standard intended to localize criminal trials and provide congressional authority where venue is otherwise indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical diversity of state court systems argues against a one-size-fits-all federal jury rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Because states vary widely—some having separate chancery, admiralty, probate, or combined jurisdictions—the federal constitution cannot easily fix a jury rule that corresponds with all states without producing irregularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: New York's distinct chancery and admiralty courts limit jury use; some states (e.g., Connecticut, Rhode Island) blend jurisdictions making jury practice broader; Massachusetts/Pennsylvania have different blends. Choosing one state's system as federal standard would provoke jealousy and opposition.
